title: Scandinavian: tactics and traps for both colours
outcomes: States the four conditions of the pin on b5 against a queen on c6 (king on e8, d7 empty, b5 guarded, no pawn block) and checks them before a queen move

Finds the check on e5 that wins the rook on a1 after the b-pawn leaves b2, and says which three features make it work (open e-file, clear diagonal, unguarded rook) after checking that nothing can take the queen
Explains the discovered attack after a bishop sacrifice on f7 against a loose bishop on g4, and names the look-alike where it fails
Separates positions with a trap from positions without one, for both colours, using the same three questions
Quotes our own counts for each trap with their sample sizes, and says what the counts do and do not show

steps.caption: White to move after 3...Qc6. Black's queen has stepped from d5 to c6. Look at the diagonal from f1 through b5 and c6 to the black king on e8, and at what is on it. What would you play?

claims.statement: Black's queen stands on c6.
No white piece attacks the queen yet.
White's bishop is still on f1.

steps.prompt: Before any explanation: write your move for White and the one thing that has to be true for it to work. You will come back to this at the end.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** A trap is a position where a natural move loses material or the initiative to one specific reply. Which traps does the Scandinavian produce for each colour, and what do they share? [I] Each is a piece on a line, with an enemy piece that can attack along that line with tempo. By the end you can state the conditions of three traps, find the look-alike where each fails, and check before you step into one.

steps.caption: The trap, step by step. Watch the diagonal that the bishop opens and what stands behind the black queen.

line.say: The bishop attacks the queen. Behind the queen the diagonal runs to the king, so the queen is pinned and cannot leave the line.
Every queen move on the line loses the queen for the bishop; ...Qxb5 at least takes the bishop first.
The knight recaptures. Black has given a queen for a bishop, about six pawns of material.

claims.statement: Against best defence the bishop move to b5 wins at least five pawns of material.
After the bishop move the queen on c6 is attacked once.
At depth 16 White stands better by about six pawns after the queen is traded for the bishop.

steps.caption: Black to move after the pin. The queen cannot step off the diagonal. Count the squares it can reach: only those on the line between the bishop and the king.

claims.statement: The pinned queen on c6 can go only to b5 (taking the bishop) or d7, both on the pin line.
It is not check: the queen itself blocks the diagonal.

steps.caption: A second way in. Black checked on e6, White answered with the bishop, and Black plays ...Qc6. Step through it.

line.say: Black attacks nothing and only steps out of the way. It looks like the same move as before.
The bishop that just blocked the check on e2 now jumps to b5 and pins the queen to the king. The same trap, one move later.

claims.statement: The move is at least 3.8 pawns worse than the best move at depth 16.
At depth 16 White stands better by about six pawns after the queen move and the pin.

steps.text: **Four conditions for the pin on b5.** [I] They must hold together. One: the queen stands on c6, the king on e8, and d7 is empty, so the queen is pinned. Two: your bishop can reach b5 along an empty diagonal. Three: b5 is guarded, so taking the bishop costs the queen. Four: no black pawn can block or capture. Ask the four questions before you move.

steps.title: Does the pin on b5 work?
steps.prompt: Predict first. The first position is the one you started with: Black's queen is on c6. In the second only the queen has moved, to d7. In the third it is on a5. For each, decide whether the bishop jump wins material, and name the square that decides it. Not sure? Use the hints for an example first.

steps.text: **What our games say about the pin.** [V] After the knight attacks the queen, 492 online games (Lichess, September 2026, all rating bands) continued with the queen on c6. White found the pin in 202 and won 182; quiet development was played 151 times and won 108. In 1,275 masters games four replies cover 1,271 (queen to a5, d6, d8 or e5), so c6 is at most four. [H] People fall for it because a queen move that dodges the knight feels like development.

steps.prompt: Do you agree with the [H]? Name a time you moved a queen out of an attack without checking what the next enemy move would hit.

steps.caption: Position after 3.b3. Black to move. Which two white pieces does a queen on e5 attack, and can White answer both?

line.say: Check along the open e-file. From e5 the queen also looks along the long diagonal to a1.
White blocks the check by developing. The rook on a1 is still attacked, and nothing guards it.
The queen takes the rook. The pawn move to b3 opened the diagonal, and the rook pays for it.

claims.statement: Against best defence the check on e5 wins at least four pawns of material.
After the check, the rook on a1 is White's only loose piece: attacked and undefended.
At depth 16 Black stands better by about three pawns or more after the queen takes the rook.

steps.text: **Why b3 fails.** [I] The move takes the b-pawn off the diagonal from e5 to a1, and the exchange on d5 had already opened the e-file. Three conditions make the check work: the e-file is open so the queen can check, the diagonal from e5 to a1 is clear, and the rook on a1 is unguarded. Also check that nothing can take the queen on e5. If one condition fails, the check is only a check.

steps.caption: A different move order to the same trap. Black answered the pawn capture with ...Nf6 instead of recapturing with the queen.

line.say: White attacks the knight on d5 from the side.
Black takes the pawn back with the knight.
The knights trade.

steps.caption: The queen recaptures on d5. Step through the same b3 and the same check.

line.say: The queen recaptures and stands on d5 again, as in the main line.
The same move as before. The long diagonal is open once more.
The same check: the move order changed, but the position has the same features.

claims.statement: After the check, the rook on a1 is White's only loose piece.

steps.title: Does the queen check on e5 win something?
steps.prompt: Predict first. The first position is the one you just saw, after b3. In the second White has played the knight to f3 instead. In the third White has played a3. Decide for each whether the check wins material, and name the feature that matters. Not sure? Use the hints for an example first.

steps.text: **What our games say about b3.** [V] After the first two moves and the queen recapture, 299 online games continued with the b-pawn to b3. White won 109 and drew 15; Black won 175. In our masters data the knight to c3, the knight to f3 and d4 cover 1,426 games, 1,275 of them with the knight to c3. [H] A fianchetto habit from other openings may explain b3, but the data cannot show why anyone chose it.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has pinned the knight on f3 to the queen with ...Bg4. Count who defends f7 and who defends the bishop on g4. What happens if the knight leaves f3 with check?

claims.statement: No black piece defends the bishop on g4.
Only the king defends the pawn on f7.
The bishop on c4 attacks f7.

steps.caption: The discovered attack, step by step. Watch what the knight uncovers when it jumps.

line.say: The bishop takes a pawn defended only by the king, with check. The king must take.
The king takes. It now stands on f7, where a knight check is waiting.
The knight leaves f3 with check. It also uncovers the queen on d1, which now attacks the bishop on g4.

claims.statement: Against best defence the bishop sacrifice nets at least one pawn of material.
After the knight jump with check, the queen on d1 attacks the bishop on g4.

steps.caption: Black to move. The king steps back, but the bishop on g4 cannot be saved.

line.say: The king steps back. Black has no time to save the bishop.
The queen takes the loose bishop. White gave a bishop and took a pawn and a bishop.

claims.statement: At depth 16 White stands better by about three pawns after the queen takes the bishop.

steps.title: Does the discovered attack work?
steps.prompt: Predict first. The first position is the one you just saw, with the bishop on g4. In the second the bishop is on f5. In both, the bishop on c4 attacks f7 and only the king defends it. What does the queen on d1 attack in each? Not sure? Use the hints for an example first.

steps.text: **What our games say about the bishop on g4.** [V] In this exact position (144 online games), White played the pawn to h3 in 40, castled in 29, played the pawn to d3 in 29 and made the sacrifice in 22, winning 15 of those 22. [I] On material alone White gains one pawn; the engine's larger number comes from Black's king losing the right to castle. The trap needs a loose bishop, so the cause is the pin habit, not the sacrifice.

steps.caption: What White plays instead of b3. The knight to c3 is the main move in our masters data, and it removes the long-diagonal trap.

line.say: The knight develops with tempo and stands on the long diagonal, so it blocks the line from e5 to a1.
The same check as before (still a real option: 87 masters games, 10,643 online [V]), but the knight on c3 now blocks the diagonal.
White blocks, develops and keeps everything guarded. No rook hangs, so the check gained nothing.

claims.statement: At depth 16 White stands slightly better after the knight move, the check and the bishop block.
After the knight move and the black check, no white piece is loose.

steps.caption: The safe move orders. Black keeps the queen off c6 and the bishop off g4, and White keeps the b-pawn on b2.

line.say: Black's most common move in masters games (598 of 1,275). The queen leaves d5 at once and stays off the pin diagonal.
White takes the centre and develops with a gain of time.
Black develops and prepares to catch up. Both sides are developing, and nobody has stepped into a trap.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the position is close to level, with White slightly ahead.

steps.caption: What Black plays instead of the pin. Develop the knight before the bishop, and the discovered attack has nothing to hit.

line.say: The knight develops first and guards g4, so a later bishop move there has a defender.
White castles. There is no loose piece and no trap; the game is an ordinary opening fight.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the position after the knight move and castling is close to level, with White slightly ahead.
After the knight move, a black piece defends g4.

steps.text: **A routine for both colours.** Before a queen move, a bishop move or a pawn move that loosens the long diagonal, ask three things. What does the enemy piece behind my piece attack if my piece moves? Which of my pieces is attacked and unguarded? Which line, diagonal or file just opened? Before you spring a trap, ask the same about the enemy. The test below mixes the patterns, and some positions have no trap at all.

**What to remember.**
- A trap is a pattern with conditions: a piece on a line, and an enemy piece that attacks along it with tempo.
- Queen on c6 with the king on e8: the bishop pins it from b5.
- Pawn on b3 opens the diagonal e5 to a1, and the exchange on d5 opened the e-file.
- A loose bishop on g4 loses to a knight jump with check.
- The look-alike fails when one condition is missing: name it.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Imagine you teach a friend who knows how the pieces move. Write five sentences: (1) the conditions of the pin on b5, (2) why b3 loses the rook, (3) what the knight uncovers on g5, (4) one look-alike where a trap fails, (5) the one question you ask before a queen move.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you name conditions rather than the names of traps? Did you say what made each look-alike fail? Did you give a position a friend could set up on a board? Did you name the colour that falls into each trap? The app grades nothing: compare your five sentences with these four questions and fix the weakest one.
